rv.q: This show, which has a genial, populist score of entertaining and empowering numbers, is not really about that plot anyway.
At least the show itself opens its arms fully, and delivers a warm, sturdy squeeze of a hug.
It’s a laugh-out-loud musical comedy with a massive dose of heart.
This show is a bona fide crowd pleaser: a warm hug that pulls you into its generous bosom.

The same can be said for the artistic team behind this appealing, tuneful and politically potent show based on Josefina López's 1990 play and the 2002 film which she co-wrote with George LaVoo, and which starred America Ferrera.
It is a bouncy, crowd-pleasing comedy about female empowerment, self-acceptance and chasing one’s ambitions.
We gossip, stitch and sweat alongside them, fully immersed in director Sergio Trujillo’s heart-expanding, joy-swollen production — yet another landmark expansion of the “Real Women” canon.

Unfortunately, there are too few other moments in Real Woman Have Curves that soar like that, that deliver the joy and delight of shaking off the many worries and fears that burden these eight women 24/7.
Put it all together and you have one spicy Mexican feast of a show – as savory as a hot tamale, smooth as flan and irresistibly tasty as a deep-fried churro.
It is a joyful, triumphant, authentic celebration of Latinidad, resilience and representation.
As “Real Women Have Curves” shows us again and again that what’s inside these women – determination, grit, compassion – is way important than what we can see with our eyes!
The musical format is a place for boldness and celebration, a chance to make this story a euphoric experience.
Audiences will leave the show feeling 1000x lighter and inspired by Ana’s journey to spread our wings, take action, and give joy.
Not only is Real Women Have Curves a joyous entertainment, it is also a moving tribute to the Mexican immigrant experience.
The realest thing Broadway has seen in quite some time.

The show is sung and performed with sincerity and heart, and its humor—particularly in family interactions and the fledgling romance of Ana and nerdy boyfriend Henry (Mason Reeves)—is tangy and sharp.
Córdoba—making a smashing Broadway debut—has us rooting for her, and the Garcias, every step of the way.
If it has a predictable plot, it’s all these women together, and the proud characters they portray in the show, that make it work.

“Real Women Have Curves” opened Sunday at the James Theatre, and it’s obvious you’re in good hands under Sergio Trujillo’s expert direction when the show kicks off with not one but two What I Want songs.

Real Women is best when allowing them to flesh out their relationships, through punchlines heartily landed, or when following Ana’s budding journalism career. Interviewing a local politician who’s quick to throw immigrants under the bus, she poignantly complains of how “everyone’s swinging right to keep up with Reagan.
Curves might not be intended as a dark treatise on American or immigrant identity, but it needn't cinch these ideas in an ill-fitting dress.
During the course of its roughly two hours, though, this real woman, at least, felt more patronized than entertained.
It’s held together by creative basting stitches, and frequently threatens to come apart at the seams.
Real Women Have Curves tells a simple story with musicality, with humor, with authenticity, and with an embrace of its female characters as fully rounded, three-dimensional individuals.

Real Women Have Curves does a great job of keeping it real– a little bit funny, a little bit cheeky, a little bit sarcastic, a little bit bold, brash, risky, exciting, infuriating, hopeful, dramatic, absurd, fun, ambitious, and brave.
Where they succeed is in their nimble use of English and Spanish, a kind of celebratory codeswitching that resonated with bilingual audience members the night I attended.
Although the two themes meld quite nicely, it is difficult for one not to distract from the other.
This has to be one of the most unappetizing moments I have seen in theater.
Overall, “Real Women Have Curves” is a mighty and weighty celebration of culture and life.

cn.t: Critics find this crowd-pleasing musical about Latina garment workers charming and timely, with strong performances and an empowering message, though some note its familiar story takes a feel-good approach over deeper dramatic complexity.
